title: Taking the Great as Allies
note: A ruler fit to drive the cart of protection takes as helpers men of great wisdom, the ministers and priests who turn him from the bad path to the good and guard him from troubles sent by people or gods.

couplets.plain: Learn how it is done, then choose with care the friendship of the wise, who know righteousness and have grown old in it.
couplets.pm: A ruler should weigh how rare it is, then find the right way to win the friendship of wise men older than himself, who know the fine points of righteousness. Older means mature in knowledge, conduct and years. The wise know sound policy and the ways of the world. The way to win them is to esteem them, raise them up and defer to them.

links.quote: who know righteousness and have grown old in it
choose with care the friendship of the wise

couplets.plain: Cherish and keep close those who can end the suffering that has come and guard against it before it comes.
couplets.pm: A ruler should please those who can remove his troubles and foresee new ones, and take them as helpers. Troubles from the gods, such as drought, flood, wind, fire and disease, are met with rites and foreseen through omens. Troubles from people, such as enemies, thieves, kin and officers, are met with the four means of statecraft. So he means priests and ministers.

links.remove: Friendship is the old English’s word. The Tamil says cherish them and take them on, and he reads that as helpers.

couplets.plain: Of all rare things the rarest is to cherish the great and make them your own.
couplets.pm: To learn what pleases the great, do it, and so make them dear to you is, for rulers, the rarest of all rare gains. Rulers can obtain everything rare in the world, and this one stands highest because through it all the others come.

links.quote: to cherish the great and make them your own
links.reason: Ranks making the great your own as the rarest thing of all.
Concerns the great themselves, and how rare it is to make them your own.

couplets.plain: Conducting yourself so that those greater than you become your own people is the highest of all strengths.
couplets.pm: For rulers, the highest of all strengths is to follow the lead of those who surpass them in wisdom and other things, so that these become dear to them. This strength of helpers is better than wealth, armies and forts, because such men can also remove troubles sent by the gods, which those can’t.

couplets.plain: A ruler goes forward with his advisers as his eyes, so he should choose them with care.
couplets.pm: A ruler carries his burden with his ministers as his eyes, so he should examine such ministers and take them as helpers. Even one who can plan alone is overwhelmed by countless tasks, and his burden goes well only through ministers whose whole work it is. Examining means testing them against the marks of a minister set out later.

links.quote: he should choose them with care

links.reason: Says what his advisers are to a ruler: the eyes he goes forward with.
A ruler goes forward with his advisers serving as his eyes.
Since a ruler goes by his advisers, they must be weighed before being taken on.

couplets.plain: If you keep worthy company and can conduct yourself well, there is nothing your enemies can do to you.
couplets.pm: Enemies can do no harm to a ruler who has worthy people around him and knows how to conduct himself. The worthy are those fit in wisdom and conduct. Conducting himself means not straying from righteousness and sound policy. Enemies work by deceit, by splitting allies, by stirring up new foes and by force, but none of this reaches one who knows and heeds those who know.

couplets.plain: If you keep companions who will rebuke you, who has the power to ruin you?
couplets.pm: What enemy in the world has the greatness to ruin rulers who value and keep helpers who come close and speak up when they see wrong? Wrong means sin and what goes against sound policy. Such helpers are free of these faults and have loving-kindness towards the ruler. They never let him stray, so no one can ruin him.

links.reason: Puts beyond ruin anyone who keeps companions able to rebuke them.

links.quote: who has the power to ruin you

couplets.plain: A ruler with no one to rebuke him has no protection, and will fall even with no one to bring him down.
couplets.pm: A ruler who doesn’t take as helpers those fit to reprove him has no protection. Even if no enemy works to ruin him, he ruins himself, like an elephant without a driver that leaves the path. “Even with no one” hints that such people will appear.

links.quote: will fall even with no one to bring him down
A ruler with no one to rebuke him

couplets.plain: Without capital there is no profit. Without a prop to lean on there is no standing firm.
couplets.pm: Merchants without capital have no profit from it. In the same way, rulers without helpers to bear them up have no stability. As you must have capital before you can profit, you must have people to hold you up before you can stand. Standing means bearing a ruler’s burden without faltering.

links.reason: As trade needs capital, standing firm needs someone to lean on.

couplets.plain: Letting go of your bond with good people is ten times worse than making enemies of many.
couplets.pm: For a ruler to fail to keep friendship with the great is ten times worse than standing alone and making enemies of many. Even with many enemies, he can get away by one means or another, setting them against each other or splitting them. Once he has let go of the good, there is no way out, so this is worse.
